title: StrictMode — What It Catches and Why It Double-Renders

subChunks.title: StrictMode — What It Catches and Why It Double-Renders
subChunks.hookHtml: You add a feature. It works in development. You deploy — and something is slightly off. Data initialised twice, a counter off by one, subscriptions stacking up. This is the kind of bug StrictMode is designed to surface before it reaches production. Understanding what it does — and why it deliberately makes your app behave differently in development — is essential for reading your own console output.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What StrictMode is

React.StrictMode is a wrapper component with no visible output. It activates extra development checks. It has zero runtime cost in production — it only runs its checks in the development build:

// main.jsx — the typical setup
import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <App />
  </StrictMode>
);

What it catches

1. Impure render functions

React components must be pure — same inputs should always produce the same output with no side effects. StrictMode detects impure renders by calling your component twice and checking if the outputs match. If your component produces different output on each call, you have a side effect lurking in your render logic.

2. Effects with missing cleanups

StrictMode mounts components, unmounts them, then mounts them again. If your effect sets up a subscription or interval without cleaning it up, you'll see it run twice in development — which is exactly how it will behave if the user navigates away and back. This surfaces missing cleanup before it causes leaks in production.

3. Deprecated API usage

StrictMode logs warnings when your app uses APIs that are deprecated or scheduled for removal in a future React version.

Vex: "StrictMode is a stress test. It applies pressure your production code will eventually face — fast navigation, hot reloads, concurrent rendering — and surfaces the cracks early. The double render is the test, not the bug."

The double-render: what you'll see

function Counter() {
  console.log('Counter rendered'); // logs TWICE in development with StrictMode
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}

In development with StrictMode: Counter rendered appears twice on mount. In production: once. This is by design. React runs your render function twice to check for side effects — if the output is the same both times, you're pure.

What this means for your code

Write render functions that are pure — no direct mutations, no timers started during render, no global variables modified during render. These should only live in event handlers or effects:

// ❌ Side effect in render — will fire twice in StrictMode:
function BadCounter() {
  externalCount += 1; // mutating outside state during render!
  return <p>{externalCount}</p>;
}

// ✅ Side effects only in event handlers and effects:
function GoodCounter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>
      {count}
    </button>
  );
}

Effect double-invocation (React 18+)

In React 18 with StrictMode, effects run twice on mount: mount → unmount → mount. This simulates fast refresh and concurrent feature behaviour. The fix is always the same: return a cleanup function from your effect:

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => setTick(t => t + 1), 1000);

  return () => clearInterval(id); // ← cleanup prevents double-interval
}, []);

If your effect doesn't need cleanup, it probably doesn't have a side effect that could double. If it does need cleanup and you haven't written it, StrictMode has just shown you the bug before your users found it.

storyBeats.text: Vex runs the same enchantment twice on a test crystal — deliberately. 'If a spell is pure, running it twice produces the same crystal,' she says. 'If the crystal changes on the second casting, there's a hidden side effect. I need to find it before the tower opens.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The double render is not a bug. It's a test. React is asking: 'Is your render function pure?' Pure means: same inputs, same output, no side effects. If your component passes the double-render test — if the output is identical both times — you're clean. If not, you have work to do.

storyBeats.speaker: Effect with cleanup prevents double-subscription

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Fix a component that has two StrictMode violations:

  • Bug 1: A side effect (mutation) happening directly in the render function — move it to an event handler
  • Bug 2: A useEffect that starts a setInterval without returning a cleanup function — add the cleanup
  • The fixed component should render a <p data-testid="tick"> with the current tick count, incrementing every second
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <PureGreeting> component that demonstrates render purity. It accepts a name prop and renders a greeting. Add a side-effect-free render body (no external mutations, no timers in render). Below it, show a counter that increments on a button click — the click handler (not the render body) should modify state. Include a comment in the code explaining why the render body is free of side effects.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a developer who is confused about why their console.log appears twice: what StrictMode is, why React deliberately double-renders in development, and what the developer should do differently as a result. Include what happens with effects and why cleanup functions matter.

questions.prompt: In development with StrictMode, a component's render function runs twice per state update. Why?
options: To detect impure render functions — if the component produces different output each call, a side effect is hiding in the render body
React renders twice to show both the old and new UI during transitions
This is a performance optimisation — React caches the second render result
StrictMode is a legacy mode that mimics React 16 behaviour
questions.answer: To detect impure render functions — if the component produces different output each call, a side effect is hiding in the render body
questions.explanation: React components should be pure functions — same inputs produce the same output. StrictMode calls your render function twice and compares outputs. If they match, the function is pure. If they differ, something in the render body has a side effect. This check only runs in development and has no production cost.

questions.prompt: In React 18 with StrictMode, a useEffect that starts a setInterval fires twice on mount, causing two intervals to run simultaneously. What is the correct fix?
options: Return a cleanup function from the effect: `return () => clearInterval(id)`
Wrap the effect in an if statement to prevent the second execution
Remove StrictMode from the app to stop the double mount
questions.answer: Return a cleanup function from the effect: `return () => clearInterval(id)`
questions.explanation: StrictMode mounts → unmounts → remounts to simulate navigation. Without cleanup, the first interval survives the unmount. The correct fix is always a cleanup function — it runs on unmount (between StrictMode's two mounts, and when the component actually unmounts). Removing StrictMode hides the bug rather than fixing it. The bug would manifest in production during navigation.

questions.prompt: StrictMode is only enabled in development. Does this mean impure components work fine in production?
options: No — React's concurrent features in production may also invoke render functions multiple times; impure components can cause real bugs in production
Yes — production React only renders each component once, so impurity is safe there
Yes — StrictMode is purely a developer experience tool with no implications for production correctness
No — StrictMode actually bundles additional checks into the production build when enabled
questions.answer: No — React's concurrent features in production may also invoke render functions multiple times; impure components can cause real bugs in production
questions.explanation: React's concurrent rendering (Suspense, transitions, streaming SSR) can pause, discard, and restart renders. An impure component — one that mutates external state during render — produces incorrect behaviour whenever React exercises this. StrictMode surfaces the problem in development, but the underlying issue exists in production too. Pure render functions are required for correctness, not just for passing StrictMode.
